findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: TL;DR second sentence: missing comma, missing article, doubled "with"
findings.quote: However we can use some tactics to achieve on-par performance with same compute budget with a few modifications.

verification.action: Read the sentence in document.txt and in the PDF (page 1, TL;DR card).
verification.outcome: The PDF shows the same wording: no comma after "However", no article before "same compute budget", and two consecutive "with" phrases.

findings.impact: This is the second sentence a reader sees; three slips in one sentence lower confidence in the care taken over the rest of the post.
findings.body_markdown:
`However we can use some tactics to achieve on-par performance with same compute budget with a few modifications.` has three slips: a sentence-opening "However" needs a comma, "same compute budget" needs "the", and the two stacked "with" phrases read awkwardly. "On par" is also not hyphenated when it follows the noun.

**Suggested Improvement:** Recast as below.
findings.suggested_edit: However, a few modifications let us achieve performance on par with the baseline on the same compute budget.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.quote: These modfications and simple yet powerful exploits to fully utilize the capabilities of modern GPUs can significantly reduce training time.

verification.action: Checked the word in the PDF (page 1) and compared with "modifications" one line above.
verification.outcome: The PDF reads "modfications"; the preceding sentence spells it "modifications".

findings.impact: A misspelling in the opening card is the first thing a proofreading reader notices.
findings.body_markdown:
`modfications` is missing an "i". The subject "These modifications and simple yet powerful exploits to fully utilize ..." is also long before the verb arrives; the edit shortens it without changing the meaning.

**Suggested Improvement:** Correct the spelling and tighten the subject.
findings.suggested_edit: These modifications are simple yet powerful exploits that fully utilize the capabilities of modern GPUs and can significantly reduce training time.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.quote: Most of it comes down to learning how GPU works.

verification.action: Read the sentence in the PDF (page 1).
verification.outcome: The PDF has the same wording; the singular count noun "GPU" has no article.

findings.impact: Small grammatical slip in the opening card.
findings.body_markdown:
`how GPU works` needs an article (or a plural). The post uses "the GPU" and "GPUs" everywhere else.

**Suggested Improvement:** Add the article.
findings.suggested_edit: Most of it comes down to learning how a GPU works.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: TL;DR headline sentence: capital "Model", missing hyphen, comma and full stop
findings.quote: We apply five one-line changes to a 124M parameter GPT-2 Model's training loop and reduce training time per step from 250 ms to 80 ms on a single RTX 5070 making training 3x faster

verification.action: Checked the sentence end in the PDF (page 1) and compared the spelling of "model" with the subtitle and the Setup list.
verification.outcome: The PDF sentence ends without a full stop and has no comma before "making". "Model" is capitalised here but lower case in the subtitle ("124M parameter model") and elsewhere.

findings.impact: This is the highlighted summary of the headline result; it is the sentence most likely to be quoted.
findings.body_markdown:
Four slips in the highlighted summary sentence: "Model's" is capitalised mid-sentence (lower case everywhere else); the compound modifier "124M parameter" needs a hyphen (also in the subtitle); a comma is needed before the participle "making"; and the sentence has no full stop in the PDF.

**Suggested Improvement:** Use the corrected sentence below.
findings.suggested_edit: We apply five one-line changes to a 124M-parameter GPT-2 model's training loop and reduce training time per step from 250 ms to 80 ms on a single RTX 5070, making training 3× faster.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Subtitle: numeral at sentence start, misplaced parenthesis, "single-line" vs "one-line"
findings.quote: 5 must-use single-line exploits that made the smallest GPT-2 (124M parameter model) train 3x faster on a consumer-grade RTX 5070 GPU.

verification.action: Compared the subtitle with the TL;DR on the same page and with the section code captions.
verification.outcome: The subtitle has "5" and "single-line exploits"; the TL;DR has "five one-line changes"; code captions have "one line". The parenthesis "(124M parameter model)" splits "GPT-2" from its noun.

findings.impact: The same five changes are named three ways within one page, and the subtitle reads as a fragment.
findings.body_markdown:
The subtitle and the TL;DR describe the same thing in different terms: `5 must-use single-line exploits` against `five one-line changes`. Pick one term ("one-line changes" is used most often) and spell out the number at the start of a sentence. The parenthesis is also misplaced: "the smallest GPT-2 (124M parameter model)" should attach "model" to GPT-2 and keep only the size in brackets.

**Suggested Improvement:** Align the subtitle with the TL;DR.
findings.suggested_edit: Five must-use one-line changes that made the smallest GPT-2 model (124M parameters) train 3× faster on a consumer-grade RTX 5070 GPU.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Mismatched punctuation around the "i.e." aside in the baseline box
findings.quote: Every tensor in this loop i.e. weights, activations, gradients — is float32.

verification.action: Read the sentence in the PDF (page 3, BASELINE box).
verification.outcome: The PDF shows the aside opened with nothing before "i.e." and closed with an em dash, so the pair does not match.

findings.impact: The sentence parses badly on first read; the reader has to back up to find where the aside starts.
findings.body_markdown:
The parenthetical list opens with a bare "i.e." and closes with an em dash. An aside needs the same mark on both sides. "i.e." is also unnecessary once the dashes are there.

**Suggested Improvement:** Use a matching pair of dashes.
findings.suggested_edit: Every tensor in this loop — weights, activations, gradients — is float32.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: ASCII arrow in prose and "triton" vs "triton-windows" in Setup

verification.action: Checked the Hardware bullet in the PDF (page 3) and compared the package name with page 9.
verification.outcome: The PDF prints a literal "->" between the prose and the command. Page 9 names the package "triton-windows"; the Setup bullet says "triton". The sentence also repeats "Windows" in two consecutive fragments ("Windows, PyTorch 2.x. Windows needs").

findings.impact: A reader may look for a package called "triton"; the arrow reads as a typing shortcut left in.
findings.body_markdown:
`Windows needs triton -> pip install ...` uses an ASCII arrow as punctuation, where the rest of the post uses the typeset arrow "→" only for measurements. The package is called `triton-windows` on page 9 but `triton` here.

**Suggested Improvement:** Replace the arrow with a colon and name the package the same way in both places.
findings.suggested_edit: Windows needs the triton-windows package: pip install -U "triton-windows>=3.8,<3.9"

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Config class and field names: GPTconfig, GPT(config), n_layers vs n_head

verification.action: Compared the page 12 listing in the PDF with its caption on page 11 and with the page 8 listing.
verification.outcome: Page 11 caption and page 12 listing: "GPTconfig" (lower-case c, not CamelCase). Page 8 listing: "GPT(config)". Within the page 12 listing the count fields are named unevenly: "n_layers" (plural) next to "n_head" (singular).

findings.impact: Readers copy these listings; a class name that breaks Python naming convention and two differently formed field names invite mismatches with the rest of their code.
findings.body_markdown:
Naming in the config listing is uneven:

- **Class name:** `GPTconfig` (page 11 caption, page 12 listing) is not CamelCase; Python convention and the source the post follows use `GPTConfig`.
- **Field names:** `n_layers` is plural while `n_head` is singular in the same listing. Use one form for both.

Locations: page 11 (`GPTconfig · python`), page 12 (`class GPTconfig:`, `n_layers: int = 12`, `n_head: int = 12`), and the instance `GPT(config)` on page 8.

**Suggested Improvement:** Rename the class in the caption and listing, and make the two count fields parallel (`n_layer`/`n_head`).

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Letter "x" in the title and TL;DR, "×" in the rest of the post

verification.action: Searched document.txt for every multiplier and checked the page 1 instances in the PDF.
verification.outcome: Letter x: title ("3x Faster"), subtitle ("train 3x faster"), TL;DR ("making training 3x faster"), all on page 1. Multiplication sign: every later instance ("8×", "1.43×", "1.5–3×", "1.74×", "7.6×", "T×T", the results table, "11×", "3.1×", "1.4×").

findings.impact: Cosmetic, but the inconsistency sits in the title and the headline number.
findings.body_markdown:
The speedup is written `3x` three times on page 1 and with the multiplication sign `×` everywhere else in the post (pages 4, 5, 8, 10, 13, 14).

**Suggested Improvement:** Use `×` throughout, including the title, subtitle and TL;DR.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Results table and chart label the same rows differently

verification.action: Compared the row labels of the results table with the chart labels directly below it in the PDF (page 13), and with the prose spelling of the vocabulary size.
verification.outcome: Table: "TF32 matmuls", "Flash attention", "vocab → 50304". Chart: "TF32", "flash attention", "vocab 50304". Prose writes the number with a thousands separator ("50,304", "50,257" on pages 4, 11, 12).

findings.impact: The table and chart show the same six rows one above the other, so the differences are visible at a glance.
findings.body_markdown:
Three of the six rows are labelled differently in the table and in the chart beneath it: `TF32 matmuls` / `TF32`, `Flash attention` / `flash attention` (capitalisation), and `vocab → 50304` / `vocab 50304`. Outside code, the vocabulary size is written `50,304` in prose but `50304` in both labels.

**Suggested Improvement:** Use one label per row in both places, for example "TF32", "Flash attention" and the label below.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw

findings.suggested_edit: Padding the vocabulary: nice numbers for

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.quote: On Ampere+ with bfloat16, PyTorch picks the flash kernel automatically.

verification.action: Searched document.txt for every mention of the GPU generation requirement.
verification.outcome: "Ampere and newer GPUs" (page 3), "The GPU is Ampere or newer" (page 4), "On Ampere or newer." (page 6), "Is the GPU Ampere or newer?" (page 14); only page 10 uses "Ampere+".

findings.impact: Minor; one informal shorthand among four spelled-out forms.
findings.body_markdown:
The hardware condition is written out as "Ampere or newer" in four places and abbreviated to `Ampere+` once. The USE IT WHEN bullets for the same condition are also not parallel: a full sentence on page 4 ("The GPU is Ampere or newer ...") and a fragment on page 6 ("On Ampere or newer.").

**Suggested Improvement:** Use the spelled-out form here and one sentence shape for the condition in each box.
findings.suggested_edit: On Ampere or newer with bfloat16, PyTorch picks the flash kernel automatically.

findings.label: Definitive Flaw
findings.summary: Glossary terms that the body text never uses

verification.action: Searched document.txt for each glossary headword outside its own glossary entry.
verification.outcome: "Boundary kernel" (page 12): body says "a separate, slower pass" and "the leftover pass". "Materialize" (page 11): body says "writing ... to memory". "FLOPs" (page 11): body says "arithmetic"; only "TFLOPS" appears, on page 4. "Gradient scaler" (page 7): body says "GradScaler". None of the four headwords occurs in the running text.

findings.impact: A glossary entry is useful only if the reader meets the term in the text; these four define words the post does not use and leave the words it does use undefined.
findings.body_markdown:
Four glossary headwords do not appear in the sections they close:

- **Boundary kernel** (page 12): the text calls it "a separate, slower pass" and "the leftover pass".
- **Materialize** (page 11): the text says "writing that T×T matrix to memory".
- **FLOPs** (page 11): the text says "more arithmetic".
- **Gradient scaler** (page 7): the text uses the class name `GradScaler`.

**Suggested Improvement:** Either use each term once in the body where the concept is introduced, or rename the glossary entry to the wording the body uses (for example the entry below).

findings.label: Potential Concern
findings.summary: "References:" label style and unidentified source types in the credits

verification.action: Compared the label with the other headings in the PDF and read the credit line above it (page 15).
verification.outcome: "References:" is plain body text with a trailing colon; the neighbouring "Related reading" and all section headings are styled headings without a colon. The credit sentence names "Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)" without saying it is a video, while "build-nanogpt" is identified as a repository. The Brown et al. entry carries a trailing note ("(GPT-3) for the optimizer settings") that no other entry has.

findings.impact: Optional polish; the list is readable as it stands.
findings.body_markdown:
Three small points in the closing card: the `References:` label is the only heading-like line with a colon and without heading styling; the credit sentence identifies `build-nanogpt` as a repository but does not say that `Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)` is a video lecture; and one of the five reference entries has an explanatory tail where the others are author, year, title only.

**Suggested Improvement:** Style the label like "Related reading" and drop the colon; write "Andrej Karpathy's video lecture Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M) and his build-nanogpt repository"; keep the reference entries to one pattern.
